name: Emoji usage — intentional or default-slop
source: Apple HIG, Icons ('Use SF Symbols in UI, not emoji', https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols) + NN/g 'Icon Usability' (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/icon-usability/)
description: A vision-LLM judges whether the overall emoji usage on the page reads as an intentional design decision (e.g., a friendly consumer app that owns its playful tone, a reaction picker, a playlist category grid where emoji ARE the design language) or as default-slop: emojis scattered across CTAs, section headers, and nav because the designer reached for them in place of committing to an icon system. This is the L3 catchall for emoji slop that the L1/L2 checks (emoji-as-icon, sparkle-ai-combo, cta-trailing-emoji) cannot judge, because it's a question of taste-in-context, not a fingerprint match.
rationale: L1 emoji checks catch specific fingerprints (sparkle+AI combo, leading emoji in headers, trailing emoji in CTAs). But they cannot answer the harder question: 'is emoji the right tool for THIS app?' A gaming site that uses 🎮 in its genre filter is making a deliberate design decision. A B2B SaaS dashboard that prefixes 'Analytics' with 📊 is using emoji because it couldn't be bothered to install heroicons. The difference lives in context: the app's voice, its audience, whether the emoji is load-bearing content or decorative filler, whether the rendering inconsistency across platforms matters for this product. Apple HIG is unambiguous that UI controls should use SF Symbols, not emoji, specifically because emoji cannot be color-controlled, cannot scale crisply, and render differently on every platform. NN/g research on icon usability emphasizes that icons must be consistent and recognizable, which emoji fail when used as UI chrome. When a vision model looks at the whole screen, it can judge whether the emoji usage reinforces the product's character or merely papers over missing design decisions.
pass_criteria: Emoji usage (if any) is either (a) absent from UI chrome (buttons, navigation, section headers, form labels) OR (b) demonstrably intentional: part of the product's voice, used consistently, load-bearing (e.g., reaction picker, category selector where the emoji IS the thing), not scattered as decoration. Fails if the judge can see emoji in multiple UI-chrome locations where a real icon system would be the craft choice, especially if different emoji appear in adjacent elements without a coherent rationale.
